parsed.explanation: Combined regime gives a visitor severe institutional exposure: national passport/visa rules require birth-sex consistency, allow refusals and possible fraud-based lifetime ineligibility; documented traveller strandings and foreign advisories. At the division, an effective criminal facility-use law reaches government buildings, public-facing private businesses and hospitals, up to a year for first offence. Parent rules bar congruent access in government-funded facilities, and federal custody/immigration custody records document birth-sex placement, conversion, hormone denial, beatings and sexual abuse. State threat framing and counterterrorism hostility heighten severity. Mitigation is partial: courts, advocacy, some state protections, existing X passports until expiry, but they do not offset active entry, facility, detention or care exposures.

entry_documents.exposure: Passports require birth-sex M/F; new X markers barred. Visa officers may refuse and seek evidence; suspected misrepresentation can trigger fraud-based ineligibility. Travellers report confiscated or blocked passports and stranding.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid; litigation, legal FAQs and some state X credentials. These do not offset foreign-passport mismatch at national entry or visa screening.
entry_documents.interaction: Document discrepancy can prompt secondary questioning, denial of admission, investigation or detention, then facility/custody exposure.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Federal corrections and immigration custody document birth-sex/conversion practices, hormone removal, forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse; arrest under facility law can lead to such custody.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: 2024 ruling preserves inmate hormone therapy in some contexts; court challenges and oversight exist, but no documented visitor-specific relief in this division.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Entry, restroom, hospital or police contact can escalate into detention where placement and medical treatment are hostile.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars transgender access to government-funded single-sex facilities. Division criminalizes birth-sex-mismatched restroom/changing rooms in government and public-facing private businesses, including hospitals; first offence up to a year.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Some exemptions for chaperoning, emergencies or out-of-order facilities may apply; suit filed; other jurisdictions protect identity. Division’s broad criminal text lacks demonstrated effective remedy.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Ordinary restroom or hospital use can become a criminal charge, document check, removal, detention and hostile placement.

care_services.exposure: Division criminalizes mismatched changing rooms in hospitals; national order blocks congruent government-funded facilities. Custody denies hormones; youth-care hostility and records subpoenas interrupt trans medical access.
care_services.protection: Private care, ombuds or emergency accommodation not documented; one ruling supports inmate hormones; local ordinances vary, not shown to override criminal facility law.
care_services.interaction: A hospital, school-health or travel-injury encounter can trigger marker scrutiny, ward refusal, disclosure or criminal exposure.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Official orders frame gender ideology as danger; counterterrorism prioritizes neutralizing groups called radically pro-transgender; schools/teachers are criminalized; reward rhetoric raises police and border hostility.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Hate-crime statutes and court challenges remain; rhetoric is not documented as an automatic arrest criterion. Civil-liberties advocacy and litigation offer some recourse.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Hostile framing can worsen every encounter: entry, restroom, hospital, police complaint, detention, school or child-care contact.

minors_guardians.exposure: Transminor in school/childcare/medical settings may be disclosed to parents within three days; national threats criminalize teachers or guardians facilitating transition; facility law reaches public buildings and hospitals.
minors_guardians.protection: Municipal protections cover some residents, and medical rights rulings exist, but no traveler-specific minor shield or guardian immunity is documented for this division.
minors_guardians.interaction: A guardian entering a school, clinic, restroom or hospital with a transminor risks outing, denial, disclosure, investigation or arrest.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No division-specific trans violence above baseline or organised street targeting is documented, but national custody abuse, facility arrests and hostile police posture create risk if stopped or outed.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Hate-crime avenues in some jurisdictions; no documented police protection or bias-recourse for trans visitors in this division; enforcement practice is uneven and unclear.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Street or facility encounters can move through police and custody, where documented outcomes include humiliation, abuse and sexual violence.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Unknowns: whether division criminal facility law remains effective, its misdemeanor/felony classification, post-suit narrowing and visitor enforcement; national passport/visa litigation and injunctions unresolved.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Courts, suits, foreign advisories, legal FAQs, legacy X passports and some state service protections exist, but not shown to give rapid, reliable traveler remedy.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Uncertain enforcement raises chance of adverse encounters and complicates getting relief before borders, restrooms, hospitals or custody events occur.

anchor_checks.comparison: This is materially lower than 0.35-A: there is no mere service exclusion—facility mismatch can be criminalized up to a year in the division, including hospitals, while national entry rules create passport/visa fraud exposure and federal custody adds documented abuse. 0.35-A has no offence.

Similar to 0.25-D, but not identical: 0.25-D features routine fraud stops and hospital placement abuse without a formal offence; here the facility exposure is explicitly criminalized and national counterterrorism/custody hostility is heavier, though division enforcement against visitors is not yet documented.

Higher than 0.15-A because gender presentation itself is not criminalized and no documented sweeps or convictions for identity alone. Courts and advocacy remain active. But the criminal facility rule, entry fraud and severe custody keep it near the top of high risk.

parsed.synthesis: The operative system combines national gatekeeping with division-level criminalization. A trans visitor can be challenged at entry over birth-sex documents, and ordinary restroom or hospital use in the division can become a criminal charge; if taken into custody, documented federal and immigration practices add birth-sex placement, hormone denial and sexual violence. Hostile threat framing and school-disclosure rules make outing consequential, especially for guardians travelling with trans minors. Positive litigation, some local protections, legacy X passports and hate-crime recourse are real but reactive and uneven. The absence of documented division enforcement under the new criminal law lowers frequency, but does not reduce the severity that discovery itself triggers.
